safety.en: Roadside traffic, bends and exposed edges need attention, and I also turned back after dogs chased me on a trail.

scenery.en: Mountains, ravines and ocean views stood out at sunrise, with the nearby dam worth a separate stop.

surface.en: I enjoyed the asphalt, while the short trail attempt is not my main running recommendation.

experience.en: I have run these roads several times and would happily return for the hills and cooler mornings.

en.title: Tenerife: San Isidro to El Rio to Arico
en.excerpt: Sunrise on winding mountain roads, two hilly runs around El Río and a spectacular ravine by Presa del Río. Good asphalt, plenty of cyclists and climbs worth taking slowly.
en.body:
I have run these roads several times now, on visits in October and November, and mornings up here are something special. The light comes over the mountains, the ocean is down below, and the road keeps giving me another climb or descent to work with. Some are steep, others much gentler. I really like that variety.

This is a different Tenerife from the [Los Cristianos and La Caleta seafront](/journal/tenerife-south-coast/). Around El Río, the air has felt cleaner to me and the temperature has often been about 4 to 5°C cooler than in Los Cristianos on my visits. That is my experience rather than a fixed difference to plan around, but it has made these roads a welcome change from the coast.

![The road entering El Río, with the village sign beside the asphalt](/assets/uploads/tenerife-el-rio-arico/el-rio-road.jpg "El Río: a base for runs in either direction along the hills.")

## Towards San Isidro and back

The longer of my two recordings goes from El Río down towards San Isidro and back, with an extra uphill section around El Río later on. It adds up to 24.1 km in total and about 460 m of climbing. The recorded line turns around on the northern approach to San Isidro, rather than continuing into its centre.

The opening kilometres on the Chimiche side are rolling rather than one continuous descent. The road runs along the inland side of the Chimiche area before the more sustained drop towards San Isidro. In this recording, the clearest downhill sections are roughly 5 to 7 km and 8 to 10 km, reaching the lowest part of the outing at around 256 m above sea level.

Coming back is where that easy downhill running turns into work. The climb away from the San Isidro side becomes noticeable around 12 to 14 km, with another sustained rise around 16 to 17 km on the way back towards the Chimiche area. Between those climbs are gentler sections where I could settle down again, but I would not describe this as a flat route.

![A sign pointing towards San Isidro beside a quiet stretch of road](/assets/uploads/tenerife-el-rio-arico/san-isidro-road-sign.jpg "Plenty of road to explore, with San Isidro signposted farther down the hill.")

The last bigger rise in this particular recording is back above El Río, around 21.5 to 22.5 km. That extra section takes the elevation to roughly 547 m before the road drops again. It is useful to see it separately on the profile: you do not have to add that hill just because I did.

![Elevation profile of the 24.1 km El Río and San Isidro-direction run](/assets/uploads/tenerife-el-rio-arico/el-rio-san-isidro-profile.svg "24.1 km including the return, with approximately 460 m of climbing. Small elevation fluctuations are filtered from the estimate.")

## Towards Arico, via La Cisnera

The other recording is 14.2 km in total, with about 340 m of climbing. It includes an uphill detour above El Río before heading along the road towards La Cisnera and Villa de Arico, then returning.

La Cisnera is the smaller place along the way. It is also named on the trail sign in my photo, which points towards La Cisnera and Villa de Arico. I initially tried the trail in that direction, but about 500 m later some dogs started chasing me. I turned around and took the asphalt instead. That happened on my outing; it is not a claim that the same dogs will always be there. In any case, I was very happy to be back on the road.

![A walking sign pointing towards La Cisnera and Villa de Arico, beside a narrow track](/assets/uploads/tenerife-el-rio-arico/trail-sign.jpg "The trail option towards La Cisnera and Villa de Arico. My run continued mainly on asphalt after I turned back.")

The first obvious effort is the climb above El Río during roughly the first 2.5 km, reaching about 580 m. The descent back towards the village then gives the legs a break. Farther along the TF-28, the road rises again on the approach to La Cisnera, around 6 to 7 km in this recording. There are smaller ups and downs towards Villa de Arico rather than one uninterrupted hill.

![A shaded pavement and colourful Arico lettering in the village](/assets/uploads/tenerife-el-rio-arico/villa-de-arico.jpg "A change of scene in Villa de Arico before the return.")

On the way back, the section from the La Cisnera side towards El Río is generally easier in elevation terms, particularly around 11 to 13 km. There are still bends and roadside stretches to pay attention to. Easier on the legs does not automatically mean there is more space to run.

![Elevation profile of the 14.2 km El Río to Arico run, including its uphill detour](/assets/uploads/tenerife-el-rio-arico/el-rio-arico-profile.svg "14.2 km including the return and detour, with approximately 340 m of climbing. The early hill and the later rise towards La Cisnera stand out.")

## Presa del Río: a reason to stop running for a moment

The nearby Presa del Río is worth a separate look. It is a concrete dam in the Barranco del Río ravine, and the rocky surroundings gave me a little Grand Canyon feeling. Not the same scale, obviously, but a very impressive view to find close to these roads.

From the trail sign in my photo, I remember reaching a turn or access towards the dam after roughly another 150 m. Treat that as a memory of the junction, not the total distance to the dam. The two running tracks below do not reach the dam wall, so I would plan this as a separate stop or walking detour rather than follow the GPX and expect it to take you there.

![A wide view from Presa del Río into the rocky ravine, with part of the concrete dam in the foreground](/assets/uploads/tenerife-el-rio-arico/presa-del-rio-landscape.jpg "Presa del Río and the ravine below it.")

Photo: [javiersanp](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Presa_de_El_R%C3%ADo_-_panoramio_%283%29.jpg), [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/).

There are walking routes around the ravine too. The [local climbing club’s account of its Presa del Río walk](https://www.cdcanariasclimb.com/circular-presa-del-rio-10-nov-24/) gives an idea of the area. I would keep sightseeing here separate from trying to maintain a running pace, especially near the drops.

## Good asphalt, but give the road your attention

Much of the pleasure for me is the winding asphalt, with mountains on one side and views towards the ocean on the other. At sunrise, it can be beautiful. The bridge and the cuttings through the rock also make it very clear that this is a road through steep terrain, not a wide coastal promenade.

![A curved road and bridge above a steep rocky ravine near El Río](/assets/uploads/tenerife-el-rio-arico/el-rio-bridge.jpg "Beautiful terrain, with exposed sections where I pay close attention to the road.")

I run beside traffic here, sometimes close to a steep edge, and cars do pass. I would keep the volume low if using headphones and leave myself room to react. I also would not assume every driver is fully alert or has seen me. [Spain’s traffic authority warns that alcohol can affect driving even within the legal limit](https://www.dgt.es/muevete-con-seguridad/evita-conductas-de-riesgo/consumo-de-alcohol/index.html), so a legal limit is no reassurance to a runner beside the road.

![Smooth asphalt winding between rock faces, with the ocean visible in the distance](/assets/uploads/tenerife-el-rio-arico/mountain-road.jpg "The sort of road I enjoy running, provided I stay aware of the bends and passing traffic.")

## More cyclists than runners

The cycling traffic reminded me of [Benissa and Moraira](/journal/benissa-moraira-fanadix/): I often felt like the only runner among the bikes. I have seen a few other runners here, but plenty more cyclists.

For someone who enjoys hills and road running, I think this area has a lot going for it. For a beginner, the climbing, roadside space and exposed sections could make it a demanding place to start. I would choose the easier southern seafront for a first relaxed holiday jog, then come up here when I wanted a different kind of run.

For me, though, these are roads I am happy to return to. Cooler mornings, long climbs, good asphalt and that ocean view from above make a very good combination.

en.seoTitle: Tenerife: San Isidro, El Río and Arico Runs | Runograph
en.seoDescription: Two personal Tenerife runs around El Río: 24.1 km towards San Isidro and 14.2 km towards Arico, with climbing profiles, maps, roadside tips and Presa del Río.

practicalSummary.goodFor: Hill training and early morning runs with mountain and ocean views.
practicalSummary.terrain: Asphalt roads with a mix of steep and gentler climbs and descents.
practicalSummary.keepInMind: Expect passing cars, bends and exposed edges; the longer climbs are demanding for beginners.
